summary: Updates the specification of the WHOIS protocol and obsoletes RFC 954, removing material that has nothing to do with the on-the-wire protocol or is no longer applicable. It does not try to change the protocol itself.

eli5.summary: A simple question-and-answer service lets you ask, "Who owns this name?" This document cleans up the old rules for asking.

subtitle: WHOIS: a simple text query over TCP port 43 that answers and hangs up.

tldr.problem: RFC 954 mixed the on-the-wire WHOIS protocol with material no longer applicable to today's Internet.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP connection to port 43, sends one text line ending in CR LF, and the server replies with text and closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 954 and documents WHOIS as it is, admitting it has no internationalisation and no strong security.

today: RFC 3912 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 954 and RFC 812, and no later RFC has replaced it.

sections.title: What WHOIS Is
sections.content:
WHOIS is a TCP-based transaction-oriented query/response protocol, originally used for 'white pages' services and information about registered domain names. It delivers content in a human-readable format.

This document obsoletes RFC 954 and removes material that is not about the on-the-wire protocol. It does not try to change the protocol or fix its shortcomings, and says a separate IETF activity (the CRISP Working Group) was addressing replacements.
sections.eli5: WHOIS is a way to ask a computer who something belongs to and get a text answer.

sections.title: The Exchange
sections.content:
A WHOIS server listens on TCP port 43. The client makes a text request, terminated with ASCII CR then LF, and the server replies with text. The reply may have several lines, so CR or LF does not mark its end.

The server closes its connection as soon as the output is finished, and that closed connection tells the client the response is complete.
sections.eli5: You ask one question, the answer comes back, and the line goes quiet when it is over.

sections.title: Protocol Example
sections.content: The RFC shows a query to the server at whois.nic.mil for 'Smith'. The client opens TCP, sends the query with CR LF, receives lines of information, and the connection is closed with FIN packets.
sections.eli5: Ask about Smith, hear what is known, then the call ends.

sections.title: Language and Security Limits
sections.content:
WHOIS has no mechanism to indicate the character set in use. US-ASCII was originally predominant, but some servers, particularly outside the USA, might use other character sets, which has harmed interoperability.

The protocol also lacks access control, integrity and confidentiality, so WHOIS services should only carry non-sensitive information intended to be accessible to everyone. The RFC adds that such a protocol would not normally be acceptable to the IETF at the time of writing.
sections.eli5: Anyone can listen in, and it does not say which alphabet it uses, so only share things that are fine for everyone to see.
